findings.title: A persisted ReviewCard with an empty options array permanently deadlocks the review session
findings.description:
`ReviewCard.options` is typed `string[]` (src/types.ts:88), which admits `[]`. Nothing between the model and this render validates it: `quiz.ts:16` casts unvalidated model JSON to `QuizQuestion[]`, `QUIZ_SCHEMA` (src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:64-72) expresses '4 options' and 'index 0-3' only in prose `description` strings that Gemini is free to ignore (no `minItems`, no bound), `QuizModal.tsx:52-61` persists every returned question verbatim, and `repo.reviewCards.listDue` re-types raw IndexedDB rows as `ReviewCard[]` with no runtime check. The compiler therefore certifies a non-empty choice list that the runtime cannot guarantee.

The concrete outcome is worse than a blank render. `options.map` at line 93 emits zero option buttons. `selected` is the ONLY state that can flip `isAnswered` (line 75), and it is set exclusively by an option button's onClick (line 99). The grade buttons — the only thing that calls `grade()` and the only thing that advances the queue (`useReviewQueue.ts:39` `setQueue(rest => rest.slice(1))`) — are rendered behind `{isAnswered && ...}` at line 125. So a card with no options renders a question with no answers and no grading controls, and the session cannot advance past it. There is no skip control. Reloading does not help: `listDue` sorts by `dueAt` ascending, so the same card returns to the head of the queue. Every other due card behind it becomes permanently unreachable and the Review feature is bricked for that profile until the user deletes the book (which is the only path that removes its cards).

Correct behavior: validate card shape at the queue boundary (non-empty `options`) and either drop or repair malformed cards, and/or make the render defensive so a card with no answerable options can still be graded/skipped. Blast radius: `useReviewQueue` -> `ReviewPage` is the whole Review feature; one malformed card from one quiz generation disables it entirely. Corroboration that the type permits this: the project's own fixture at `src/features/review/reviewQueue.test.tsx:149` constructs `newCard({ options: [], correctAnswerIndex: 0 })` and it type-checks cleanly — but that test only exercises deletion, so no test renders this state.

findings.title: correctAnswerIndex is never bounds-checked against options.length, so a card can be silently impossible to answer correctly
findings.description:
`ReviewCard.correctAnswerIndex` is a bare `number` (src/types.ts:89) with no bound relating it to `options.length`, and it arrives from the same unvalidated path as F01 (model JSON cast at `quiz.ts:16`, persisted by `QuizModal.tsx:58`, re-typed from IndexedDB by `repo.reviewCards.listDue`). The schema's '0-3' constraint is a prose `description` (src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:71), not an enforced range. Nothing in `useReviewQueue` or `ReviewPage` checks `0 <= correctAnswerIndex < options.length`.

Worth being precise about the failure mode: `ReviewPage` never does `options[correctAnswerIndex]`, so there is no `undefined` render and no crash. It compares indices (lines 76 and 94). With an out-of-range index (say 7 against 4 options, or a negative), `showCorrect` is false for every rendered option and `isCorrect` is false for every possible selection. The user answers, no option is highlighted green, whatever they picked is highlighted red, and the explanation claims a correct answer that is not on screen. The card is permanently un-answerable-correctly and stays in rotation being marked wrong forever. Because the user can still grade it, this degrades quietly rather than blocking — which is why it is likely to go unnoticed and unreported.

Correct behavior: validate the index against the options array at the boundary where cards enter typed code, and model the pair as a single validated unit rather than two independent primitives. Blast radius: every card produced by quiz generation; the identical unguarded comparison also exists in `QuizModal.tsx:78` and `:183`, so the same malformed data misbehaves in the in-quiz flow too.

findings.title: useReviewQueue has no return annotation, so `current` is inferred as a definite ReviewCard while the runtime returns undefined
findings.description:
`useReviewQueue` is exported with no explicit return type, so its contract is whatever TypeScript infers from the returned object literal. With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off (tsconfig.json sets only `strict: true`), `queue[0]` infers as `ReviewCard`, not `ReviewCard | undefined`. The hook's public type therefore states that `current` is always a card — which is false for the overwhelmingly common case of an empty queue (nothing due), and false on first paint before `reload()` resolves.

No crash today: `ReviewPage.tsx:52` guards with `if (!current)` and renders the 'Nothing due' state, and `useReviewQueue.ts:36-37` guards internally with `const [current] = queue; if (!current) return;`. Both guards are correct — and both are, as far as the compiler is concerned, dead code testing a value that can never be falsy. That is the actual danger: the type actively argues against the only thing keeping the feature alive. A second consumer (a nav badge doing `current.question.slice(0, 40)`, a keyboard-shortcut handler, a test helper) gets zero compiler pressure to guard and throws `Cannot read properties of undefined`. Equally, enabling `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-condition` — not currently configured in eslint.config.js, which runs untyped rules only — would report both existing guards as removable, inviting a 'cleanup' that turns the empty-queue path into a hard crash on the Review page.

Correct behavior: annotate the hook's return with `current: ReviewCard | undefined` (or enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) so the guard is required rather than tolerated. Blast radius: currently one consumer (`ReviewPage`), so this is refactor-safety rather than a live defect; the fix is trivial and makes both existing guards provably load-bearing.

findings.title: ProfileContextValue models loading and profile as independent fields, so the type permits acting on a null profile mid-load
findings.description:
`ProfileContextValue` exposes `profile: Profile | null` and `isLoading: boolean` as orthogonal fields. The three states that actually exist — loading (profile not yet known), settled-with-profile, settled-without-profile — are encoded as four representable combinations, and the compiler cannot tell them apart. `profile === null` is ambiguous between 'still loading' and 'no profile selected', which is exactly the failure CLAUDE.md records as learned the hard way: 'Hooks that depend on the profile must wait for useProfile().isLoading to settle, or they will act on a null profile and silently drop the write.' The type does not enforce that rule; it is documentation only, which is why `useLibrary.tsx:25` and `useReviewQueue.ts:14` each hand-roll the same `if (profileLoading) return;` line with a comment explaining why.

Blast radius: 10 non-test consumers of `useProfile()`. Only 3 read `isLoading` (`App.tsx:10`, `useLibrary.tsx:18`, `useReviewQueue.ts:9`). The other 7 — `useTheme.ts:15`, `AppShell.tsx:26`, `ProfilePage.tsx:8`, `ProfilePicker.tsx:7`, `LibraryPage.tsx:17`, `BookDetailPage.tsx:14`, `ReaderPage.tsx:10` — destructure `profile` and treat `null` as 'no profile', with the type raising no objection.

Honest scoping: there is no live bug, because `App.tsx:12-18` gates the entire tree on `isLoading` before rendering anything, so no consumer in this lot can observe the loading state. That single gate is the only thing making the other 7 consumers correct, and it is invisible to the type system. Move it, add a route outside it, or render any of these components in a test/Storybook harness without the gate, and the silent-drop class returns with no compiler error — e.g. `useTheme.setTheme` (useTheme.ts:33-39) returns `Promise<void>` that resolves as if the write succeeded while `if (!profile) return;` discards it.

Correct behavior: a tagged union (`{ status: 'loading' } | { status: 'ready'; profile: Profile } | { status: 'no-profile' }`) so `profile` is only reachable after narrowing, making the gate compiler-enforced instead of convention-enforced. Verified negatives in this file: `createContext<ProfileContextValue | undefined>(undefined)` (line 20) is honest — no `null as unknown as T` default — and `useProfile()` throws outside the provider (line 113) and annotates its return explicitly.

findings.title: An unvalidated Profile.theme from IndexedDB is annotated into a three-literal union it may not belong to
findings.description:
`const theme: ThemeChoice = profile?.theme ?? 'system'` is the point where an unvalidated persisted value acquires a narrow type. `Profile` records come from `repo.profiles.list()`, which re-types raw IndexedDB rows without any runtime check, so `profile.theme` is `unknown` in practice. The `??` handles only null/undefined; a value like `"Dark"`, `"sepia"` or `"null"` passes straight through, and the explicit `ThemeChoice` annotation certifies to the compiler that it is one of `'system' | 'light' | 'dark'`. Line 27 then inherits the lie: the ternary's else-branch is believed to be `'light' | 'dark'` and is annotated `ResolvedTheme`, so `resolved` is typed as a two-literal union while holding an arbitrary string.

Concrete outcome (silent, not a crash): `classList.toggle('dark', resolved === 'dark')` at line 30 evaluates false, so the app renders in light mode with no error and no way for the user to tell why. In `ThemeToggle.tsx:24-26` the `theme === value` comparison is false for all three buttons, so `aria-pressed` is false on every one — the control group shows nothing selected, and a screen-reader user gets no current-state announcement. Clicking any button repairs it, so it self-heals on interaction.

Honest severity note: I traced every in-app writer and none can produce an out-of-union value. `repo.profiles.create` defaults `theme: input.theme ?? 'system'` (repo.ts:23); `useTheme.setTheme` only writes a `ThemeChoice`; `migrate.ts`'s `LegacyProfile` has no `theme` field at all, so migrated profiles get the default. The realistic vectors are a hand-edited IndexedDB record, a shared/downgraded browser profile, or a future theme value ('sepia' is a plausible addition given EReader owns its own reader themes) written by a newer build and read by an older one. Hence Low. The fix is a small parse-at-the-boundary guard rather than an annotation. Blast radius: `useTheme` is called at the shell level (`AppShell.tsx:31`) so it governs the whole app's dark mode.

findings.title: StatsPage destructures books without isLoading, so an unloaded library is typed identically to an empty one
findings.description:
`useLibrary()` returns `books: Book[]` alongside a separate `isLoading: boolean`, and `StatsPage` takes only `books`. `Book[]` cannot express 'not loaded yet', so the empty array returned before `reload()` resolves is indistinguishable — to the compiler and to the component — from a genuinely empty library. The type offers no prompt to check `isLoading`, and unlike `BookDetailPage.tsx:19` and `ReaderPage.tsx:14` (which do gate on `isLoading`), this page does not.

Concrete outcome: on navigation to /stats the user briefly sees a fully-rendered, confidently-wrong dashboard — 'Finished 0 out of 0', 'Total Learning 0m', 'Avg. Rating 0', 'No category data available yet', and the Wisdom Milestone copy reading 'enough knowledge to discuss deep concepts for over 0 hours straight' — which then flips to real numbers once IndexedDB responds. It reads as data loss for the instant it is on screen.

Verified negatives worth recording, because they were plausible and are not true: `StatsView` is arithmetic-safe on an empty array. Both `reduce` calls pass an initial value of 0 (StatsView.tsx:17, 20) so neither throws `TypeError` on an empty array; `avgRating` is guarded by `finished.length > 0` (line 19) so there is no NaN; and the only division by `stats.total` (line 153) sits inside a map over `categoryData`, which is empty whenever `total` is 0, so it never evaluates. No NaN and no throw — the defect is purely the untagged loading state.

Correct behavior: gate on `isLoading` here as the book pages do, or model the library state as a tagged union so the compiler forces the distinction. Blast radius: this page only; the underlying untagged loading bag in `useLibrary` is the shared root cause.
